column15: Micro-distillery on Sanday, Orkney; mothballed since 2023 and, per a December 2025 Food Standards Scotland warning, told consumers not to buy or drink ANY of its products (whisky, gin or new-make) over safety-regulation failures. Uses Orcadian bere barley. No characterized whisky exists to assess peat.

Built 1990 on Balvenie's site, sharing Balvenie's mash house/washbacks; output mostly feeds Grant's blends (Clan MacGregor). No source directly states its own peat level, so left unknown rather than inferred from the unpeated Balvenie link. Historically its single malt was released as 'Hazelwood' (tribute bottlings, pre-2013); the company began official 'Kininvie'-branded releases in 2013. Since 2015 'House of Hazelwood' is a revived line but is a BLEND featuring Kininvie among other Grant's malts, not itself a Kininvie brand, so no separate brand row was created for it - flag for a human reviewer if 'Hazelwood'/'House of Hazelwood' turns out to be a catalogue brand string.

Pre-production as of this research: official site states construction completed summer 2025 and distilling was expected to begin H2 2025, aiming to revive an 'old style' single malt not made since the 1960s. No product exists yet to characterize. The site's own copy calls this a return to 'old style Highland distilling' (likely the traditional method, not the SWA legal region) - the given region (Lowland) is used unchanged per instructions.

Still under construction as of the source's Jan 2026 snapshot (a cited construction-news article projected 2025 completion); no new-make spirit reported yet, so no peat basis exists. Owner Ian Macleod Distillers also markets the heavily-peated Islay blend 'Smokehead' (sourced from an undisclosed third-party distillery, not their own), so an Islay-peated future house style is plausible but is NOT claimed here.

Official site (lerwickdistillery.com redirects to shetlandwhisky.com) brands itself 'Home of Shetland Single Malt Scotch Whisky' and sells a 'Haad Still' cask-ownership scheme, consistent with stock still maturing rather than a released, characterized product. No peat statement found. Per Wikipedia's Kimbland article this distillery was established in Shetland in 2022.

Diageo's experimental/R&D distillery (est. 2013, Diageo's 29th working distillery) attached to the world's biggest bottling/packaging plant - built for pilot distillation projects, not a defined consumer single-malt line, so no house peat style is established. 'Leven' is also a common Scottish place name; kept the alias brand-scope for collision safety per this task's instructions.

First single malt (MCDXCIV) released 2021; no peat statement found in Wikipedia or a quick check of the official site. Site of the 1494 Exchequer Rolls entry, the earliest surviving written record of Scotch whisky distilling.
Working farm distillery in Ayrshire; inaugural single malt Oct 2021, a cask-strength release May 2023, 'Our Barley' Jan 2025. No peat statement found.

First whisky cask filled March 2024 (unusual wood-fired stills, worm-tub condensers); too young for a released/characterized single malt as of this research. Originally founded 2017 as the 'Dark Sky Spirits' independent bottler before building its own distillery in Moffat, Dumfries and Galloway.

No dedicated Wikipedia article; two guessed official domains (northpointdistillery.com, northpointdistillers.com) both answered 200 but rendered no readable text on a plain fetch (JS-heavy site), so no citable content was found either way.

Official site confirms its whisky ('Uist Whisky') is 'soon to launch' as of this research, with a 2026 founders-club cask scheme still selling - no released/characterized spirit yet. Their existing product line is the 'Downpour' gin range (a different brand name, gin only, out of scope here).

IMPORTANT correction to this task's framing: Orkney Distilling Ltd's flagship 'Kirkjuvagr' name is GIN ONLY (confirmed via the official site's own product navigation: 'Kirkjuvagr Gin', 'Special Edition Gin') - it is NOT their whisky brand. Their actual whisky is sold as 'Fara' and 'Rysa' (both labelled Blended Malt Scotch Whisky, i.e. vatted from multiple distilleries' malt, not a single-distillery malt of their own), added below as separate kind=blend rows with real peat citations from the same official site. This distillery-level row is left peatProfile=unknown since the range spans both an unpeated line (Fara) and a lightly-peated one (Rysa) - never averaged, per this task's own sibling-brand rule. Collision safety: the catalogue's 'An Orkney'/'Cask Orkney'/"Probably Orkney's Finest" are Highland Park or undisclosed, NOT this company - alias kept brand-scope.

Orkney Distilling Ltd's core Blended Malt Scotch Whisky, named for the uninhabited Orkney island of Fara. Official site describes it with sweet heather-honey, vanilla and spiced-apple notes; no peat mentioned, unlike its sibling Rysa.

Orkney Distilling Ltd's peated Blended Malt Scotch Whisky, named for the uninhabited Orkney island of Rysa. Official site: 'Gentle peat smoke meets rich dried fruit and creme brulee sweetness, with hints of burnt leather and pepper' - a gentle/light peat, not a heavy one.

Diageo's own site (malts.com) describes it as having an 'elegant, peated coastal character' and calls the whisky 'prized for its rarity and refined peated character' - confirms peated but not an exact intensity. Classed 'heavy' rather than 'medium' on well-established historical consensus grouping it with Lagavulin/Caol Ila (same regional maltings/era) rather than Highland Park/Bowmore's medium tier - a reviewer may want a source with an explicit ppm figure. Closed 1983, reopened 2024; one of the most sought-after 'ghost distilleries' among independent bottlers for decades.

UK's first vertical distillery (Edinburgh; opened to the public Oct 2023, but new-make production only began early 2024) - under the 3-year minimum, so no legal Scotch has been released yet to characterize.

The distillery's own name is 'Pulteney' (est. 1826, Wick); 100% of its retail output is marketed as 'Old Pulteney'. An existing out/02/producer.tsv row already covers slug=old-pulteney (kind=distillery, no parentSlug, peatProfile=none/high) - this row is added alongside it so an independent bottler's cask labelled the bare distillery name 'Pulteney' (without 'Old') still resolves, exactly the Gordon & MacPhail Ledaig-style pattern this whole task targets. ARCHITECTURE NOTE for a human reviewer: ideally old-pulteney would carry kind=brand + parentSlug=pulteney to match the intended distillery/brand split (see this task's own worked example for Pulteney/Old Pulteney) - I have not edited that file, only flagged it here. Wikipedia: marketed 'The Genuine Maritime Malt', character attributed to sea-air exposure during maturation; no peat mentioned anywhere in the article.

Official site: the flagship single malt is 'Lightly peated and balanced with rich, dark fruit flavours' - a deliberate house style combining peated and unpeated new-make. First legal whisky released Sept 2020; the earlier 'While We Wait' releases (2017-2020) were independently-bottled previews, not the distillery's own matured spirit.

Classic triple-distilled Lowland malt, historically dubbed 'King of the Lowlands'; Wikipedia describes its character as fruits, grasses and flowers, with no peat mention anywhere in the article. Closed 1993 (original stills stolen 2008/09), trademark and site acquired by Ian Macleod Distillers in 2017, rebuilt and reopened 2023. One of the most famous 'ghost distilleries' among independent bottlers for the decades it was closed.

Wikipedia titles this article 'Saxa Vord distillery' but describes it as a GIN distillery (Unst, Shetland) releasing under the 'Shetland Reel' brand; a proposed single-malt whisky distillery announced in 2018 had not raised construction funding as of the article's 2022-sourced text, so it is unclear whether they now distil their own whisky at all - a reviewer may want to check for a post-2022 update. They separately released independently-bottled whisky under the Shetland Reel name in 2015, sourced from Glenglassaugh casks and finished on-site - not their own distillate, and possibly a one-off rather than an ongoing line. peatProfile left unknown since no own-distilled whisky (peated or not) is confirmed. See the 'Shetland Reel' alias below, pointed at this row for that reason.

No dedicated Wikipedia article; parent company Dunnet Bay Distillers' official site (checked this session) shows only its established gin/vodka/rum range (Rock Rose Gin, Holy Grass Vodka, Mapmaker's Rum) with no live whisky operation or 'Stannergill' mention anywhere - consistent with a very early-stage or announced-only project. No basis for any peat claim.

Confirmed correct entity via the owner match (June and Cameron McCann). First whisky new-make run Oct 2023 - reported as the first whisky distilled in Stirling since 1852; no peat statement found. Currently better known for Stirling Gin (stocked in Co-op since 2024) than for its whisky, which may not yet be legally aged Scotch.

Small craft distillery (2013), acquired by independent bottler Douglas Laing & Co in 2019 (first Strathearn single malt under the new ownership, 'The Heart', released 2022). Also blends a honey-based whisky. No peat statement found in the source checked.

Diageo Speyside malt distillery (Keith) whose output is used 'primarily for the production of blends such as J&B whisky' per Wikipedia; the article covers history/ownership only and states nothing about flavour or peat either way, so left unknown rather than assumed from Speyside/blending-component convention.
First single malt released Jan 2025 (matured across virgin oak, Heaven Hill bourbon and two oloroso sherry casks; 800 bottles); also makes gin, corn whisky and rye whisky. No peat statement found.

No dedicated Wikipedia article; the official site (toulvaddiedistillery.com) answered 200 but rendered only script/style content on a plain-text fetch (JS-heavy site), so no citable content was retrieved. No information found on production status or peat.

No dedicated Wikipedia article beyond the list page (which places it in Inverness, Highland, matching the given region); no official site resolved under an obvious domain guess. Name is Scottish Gaelic for 'monster'. No information found on production status or peat.
John O'Groats, Caithness; first spirit run 2022, officially opened by King Charles III in Aug 2023. No peat statement found in the Wikipedia article.

Conventional column-still grain whisky distillery (Easter Ross; est. 1959, operating from 1961), feeding Whyte & Mackay blends alongside Tamnavulin. Grain whisky is produced from unmalted cereal via continuous distillation and is not peated. No official single-grain release from the owner, but independent bottlers (e.g. Signatory, Douglas Laing) commonly release single-cask 'Invergordon' single grain - exactly the gap this row exists to close.

Mossburn's own site contrasts its two distilleries directly: 'Torabhaig and Reivers are poles apart, sitting at opposite ends of the whisky-making spectrum' - Torabhaig makes 'an extremely characterful, peated new-make spirit', so Reivers (first Single Grain Scotch Whisky planned for 2020, Scottish Borders) is positioned as its unpeated opposite. Note: this URL currently returns HTTP 404 despite serving this real page content (a site-routing quirk on their end) - a human reviewer may want to re-check it lands correctly.

Large grain whisky distillery plus vatting/blending/bottling plant (Livingston, West Lothian; 25 million litres/year capacity) feeding La Martiniquaise's blends. Conventional column-still grain whisky, not peated.

Wikipedia: 'there is no official bottling. However, the Scotch Malt Whisky Society and other independent bottlers have purchased and bottled some aged casks of this as Single Cask Single Grain whisky' - confirms real independent-bottler activity (the exact scenario this research batch targets) for this conventional, unpeated grain whisky distillery (Gorbals, Glasgow; est. 1927).
